newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker on softening dollar.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker on softening dollar.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker in moderate trade on Friday as pre-election weakness in the Canadian dollar fed through to the money market, analysts said.

"The reason that the dollar is a little weaker and the (money) market is a little weaker is that there's just a little bit of fear coming into the market about a minority government," said one T-bill trader with bank-owned brokerage.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.05 percent from 3.04 percent at the close of trading on Thursday.

The Canadian dollar opened slightly weaker at C$1.3819 (US$0.7236) in light trading on Friday. Dollar traders said the currency would remain volatile as long as there were doubts the governing Liberals would win enough suppport for a parliamentary majority in Canada's June 2 general election.
An Angus Reid Group poll broadcast by CTV News on Thursday night showed support for the Liberals at 36 percent, a substantially weaker level than indicated in recent polls.
"There is that nervousness, as you always get before an election, and anything like that is going to make everybody back off a little," said the T-bill trader.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.37 percent from 3.36 percent. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 3.86 percent from 3.85 percent.
The call loan rate traded at 3.05 percent, near the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range.
